pitfall_name: WebGPU buffer readback synchronization counted as compute time
what_happens: Benchmarks that wrap the entire proving function report 2-5x slower 'GPU time' than actual shader execution because the timer includes mapAsync() stalls waiting for GPU→CPU memory copies, PCIe latency, and GPU idle time during synchronization fences.
why: WebGPU compute shaders execute asynchronously on the GPU queue. When a proving step requires reading an intermediate commitment back to CPU for Fiat-Shamir hashing (common in SNARKs), mapAsync() inserts a CPU-blocking synchronization point. The GPU may have finished the kernel milliseconds earlier, but the benchmark timer keeps running until the CPU sees the data.
how_discovered: Profile shows GPU idle for 60-80% of the measured 'compute' interval; removing the readback and running two back-to-back dispatches without mapping drops the per-proof time by 3x. Typically wastes 1-2 days before someone runs a GPU profiler (Chrome's about:tracing or PIX) and sees the queue gap.
mitigation: Measure only the dispatch-to-dispatch interval using GPU timestamp queries (where available), or structure the benchmark to batch multiple proofs between readbacks. Report 'kernel time' and 'end-to-end time' as separate metrics.

pitfall_name: GPU timestamp-query quantization in Chrome (100 µs default)
what_happens: Microbenchmarks of individual GPU kernels report quantized durations in 100 µs buckets, making kernels faster than ~200 µs appear to take identical time regardless of actual shader changes.
why: Chrome quantizes GPU timestamp-query results to 100 microseconds by default as a Spectre-class timing-attack mitigation. The 'enable-webgpu-developer-features' flag disables quantization, but most end-user browsers run with it enabled. The quantization granularity is larger than the execution time of many proving subroutines (MSM buckets, NTT butterflies).
how_discovered: Repeated runs of a supposedly-optimized kernel show identical durations (e.g., always 0.10 ms or 0.20 ms) while shader compilation changes produce no measurable delta. Usually wastes half a day before the developer notices the distribution is stair-stepped.
mitigation: Run benchmarks in Chrome with --enable-features=WebGPUDeveloperFeatures, or accumulate many kernel iterations between queries and divide. Never trust sub-millisecond GPU timings from default Chrome.

pitfall_name: WASM JIT tiering distortion (Liftoff → TurboFan in V8)
what_happens: The first proving run is 3-8x slower than the second because the initial execution uses the unoptimized Liftoff compiler; subsequent hot-loop recompilation through TurboFan produces vectorized, optimized code.
why: V8 compiles WASM modules first through Liftoff (single-pass, fast compile, no optimizations) to minimize startup latency. After a function becomes hot, it is recompiled by TurboFan (optimizing compiler with register allocation, SIMD lowering, and inlining). A cold-start benchmark measures Liftoff performance, which is irrelevant for sustained proving workloads.
how_discovered: The second benchmark run is mysteriously 4x faster with no code changes; adding a 5-iteration warmup before measurement stabilizes results. Typically wastes a full day while the developer suspects cache effects or memory allocation.
mitigation: Always include an explicit warmup phase (≥5 full proof iterations or ≥30 seconds of compute) before collecting timings. Report whether the benchmark was cold-start or steady-state.

pitfall_name: JS GC pauses during witness marshalling attributed to proving time
what_happens: Benchmarks measuring from JS show sporadic 50-500 ms spikes that are recorded as 'proving time' but are actually V8/SpiderMonkey garbage collection pauses triggered by temporary TypedArray and BigInt allocations during witness serialization.
why: When converting a JS witness object (e.g., arrays of decimal strings) into a WASM-readable linear memory buffer, the JS shim often creates many intermediate Uint8Array slices, BigInt temporaries, or ArrayBuffer instances. These allocate on the JS heap; when the heap fills, a mark-and-sweep or generational GC pause freezes the main thread. If performance.now() calls bracket the entire JS→WASM→prove→JS pipeline, the GC pause is counted as proof time.
how_discovered: Chrome DevTools Memory profiler shows GC events aligned with the timing spikes; moving witness construction outside the benchmark interval eliminates the spikes. Usually wastes 2-3 days because the developer first suspects WASM memory growth or thread contention.
mitigation: Pre-allocate a reusable WASM memory buffer and write witness data into it directly without intermediate JS objects. Measure proving time from inside WASM (or exclude JS marshalling from the timed region).

what_happens: In non-cross-origin-isolated contexts, performance.now() resolution is clamped to 100 µs or coarser, making it impossible to distinguish between a 1.2 ms and a 1.3 ms proving step.
why: Browsers reduce timer resolution as a Spectre mitigation unless the document is cross-origin isolated (COOP/COEP). Proving workloads that have not yet deployed the required headers (or are embedded in contexts that cannot serve them) get coarse timers. The clamping rounds sub-millisecond differences, destroying statistical power for A/B optimization tests.
how_discovered: Benchmark histograms show discrete 0.1 ms buckets with no variance; running the same code in a cross-origin-isolated tab restores expected Gaussian noise. Usually wastes a few hours before the developer checks navigator.crossOriginIsolated.
mitigation: Ensure COOP: same-origin and COEP: require-corp headers are served. If impossible (e.g., embedded widget), use larger iteration counts and measure total duration to amortize quantization error, or use WASM-side timing via instruction-count approximations.

pitfall_name: WASM 32-bit 4 GiB memory ceiling for large circuits
what_happens: Proofs for circuits with >100M constraints or large witness vectors crash with RangeError or OOM during memory.grow() because 32-bit WASM is capped at 4 GiB (actually ~2-3 GiB usable due to allocator overhead), and Memory64 is unsupported in Safari.
why: WASM MVP uses 32-bit memory indices (i32), limiting linear memory to 4 GiB. The Memory64 proposal extends this to 64-bit, but Safari (both macOS and iOS) does not implement it as of 2026. Even on Chrome/Firefox, Memory64 requires toolchain support (Rust nightly, specific Emscripten flags) that many proving libraries have not adopted. Large proving keys, SRS files, and witness data easily exceed this limit.
how_discovered: memory.grow() returns -1 (failure) or the runtime throws RangeError: WebAssembly.Memory.prototype.grow() failed. Developer initially suspects a memory leak before checking memory.buffer.byteLength and realizing it is pinned near 4 GiB. Typically wastes 1-2 days.
mitigation: Use Memory64 on supported browsers with a 64-bit toolchain. On Safari, fall back to disk-backed paging or split the proof into smaller recursive circuits. Avoid loading the full SRS into WASM memory; stream or window it.

pitfall_name: SharedArrayBuffer COOP/COEP deployment friction in embedded contexts
what_happens: WASM threads (required for parallel MSM/NTT) cannot spawn because SharedArrayBuffer is unavailable, and the page cannot obtain cross-origin isolation when embedded inside a cross-origin iframe or a CDN that does not allow custom headers.
why: SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation (COOP + COEP). If the proving application is embedded as a wallet widget in a third-party dApp via cross-origin iframe, the parent page controls the headers. Many hosting platforms (GitHub Pages, default S3, some CDNs) do not support setting COOP/COEP. Without SAB, WASM threads abort at instantiation.
how_discovered: WebAssembly.instantiate() throws LinkError: WebAssembly.Memory() cannot be created with maximum size; or the threads polyfill fails. Developer checks console and sees 'SharedArrayBuffer is not defined'. Usually wastes half a day before realizing the iframe parent lacks the headers.
mitigation: Use a credentialless iframe (Chromium-only) or require the embedding page to serve COOP/COEP. Alternatively, implement a single-threaded fallback path and detect SAB availability at runtime.

pitfall_name: SIMD128 misfit with wide prime-field Montgomery multiplication
what_happens: Enabling WASM SIMD128 produces no speedup (or a slowdown) for finite-field arithmetic because 254-bit prime-field elements do not align with 128-bit vector lanes, and compilers fail to auto-vectorize carry-handling Montgomery code.
why: WASM SIMD128 operates on four 32-bit or two 64-bit lanes per vector. A 254-bit field element requires 4×64-bit limbs or 8×32-bit limbs. Montgomery multiplication involves lane-crossing carries and conditional reductions that do not map to SIMD shuffle/blend patterns. The compiler (LLVM/Emscripten) emits scalar fallback code, and the SIMD instruction fetch/decode overhead slightly regresses performance compared to compact scalar i64 code.
how_discovered: Benchmark shows identical cycle count with and without -msimd128; disassembling the WASM reveals no v128 instructions in the hot loop (or inefficient splat/shuffle sequences). Typically wastes 2-3 days of attempted vectorization before accepting scalar i64 is faster for this field width.
mitigation: Write hand-optimized SIMD intrinsics only if the field fits in 2×64-bit (e.g., 128-bit fields). For 254-bit fields, prefer scalar i64 with inline assembly or compiler builtins, and profile to confirm SIMD is actually used in the hot loop.

pitfall_name: Safari WebGPU compute shader gaps and TBDR timestamp limitations
what_happens: Proving workloads that run on Chrome/Firefox fail or produce incorrect results on Safari because Safari's WebGPU implementation uses Tile-Based Deferred Rendering (TBDR) with compute-shader restrictions, and timestamp-query only supports atStageBoundary sampling.
why: Safari implements WebGPU on top of Metal, which is TBDR on Apple Silicon. Compute shaders may have reduced threadgroup memory, different barrier behavior, and dispatch-size limits compared to Chrome's Dawn/Vulkan backend. Additionally, Safari only supports timestamp-query at stage boundaries (not at draw/dispatch boundaries), making kernel-level profiling impossible. Safari also lacks Memory64 support, compounding memory limits.
how_discovered: Code works in Chrome but produces wrong commitment hashes or hangs in Safari; Safari GPU process logs show Metal validation errors. Timestamp queries return zero or coarse values. Usually wastes 1-3 days of Safari-specific debugging.
mitigation: Test compute shaders on Safari early; avoid relying on dispatch-size tuning from Chrome. Use Metal-specific workgroup sizes (multiples of 32 threads). Do not depend on per-dispatch GPU timestamps in Safari—use CPU wall-clock as fallback.

pitfall_name: Mobile browser tab memory kills (iOS Safari ~1.5 GiB limit)
what_happens: Proving aborts mid-computation on iOS Safari with a generic 'This webpage was reloaded because a problem occurred' or the tab simply reloads, losing all in-progress state.
why: iOS Safari imposes a hard per-tab memory limit (approximately 1.5-2 GiB depending on device RAM). Proving workloads with large SRS files, witness vectors, and WebGPU buffers quickly exceed this. Unlike desktop browsers, iOS does not swap; it immediately kills the WebContent process. Android Chrome is more permissive but still kills heavy tabs under memory pressure.
how_discovered: Tab reloads reproducibly at the same proof size threshold; Safari Web Inspector shows memory climbing to ~1.4 GiB just before the crash. Desktop Chrome handles the same proof fine. Usually wastes a day before the developer tests on actual hardware instead of simulator.
mitigation: Cap circuit size for mobile; use recursive proof composition to keep per-proof memory under ~800 MiB. Monitor performance.memory (where available) and gracefully degrade to a server-side proof or smaller circuit. Never assume desktop memory limits apply to mobile.
